newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian PM seeks support for reform programme.
newsitem.headline: Romanian PM seeks support for reform programme.

text.p: Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said on Tuesday Romania had no choice but to back his centrist government's painful market reforms to hoist the economy out of its post-communist tailspin and boost living standards.

"We are convinced that the reform programme is the only way to emerge from the crisis still gripping Romanian society," Ciorbea told parliament in a debate seeking formal approval of reforms four months after they were launched.
"Taking formal responsibility for the programme means political leaders are taking a step towards their fellow citizens."
Parliament's two chambers, heavily dominated by centrists who ousted ex-communists in last November's general election, are certain to back the programme.
The leftist opposition, accused by ministers and Western lenders of stalling reforms during seven years in office, have submitted a confidence motion to be debated later this week.
Ciorbea said the government's reforms had already begun to take effect, with restrictions removed from exchange markets and most prices freed from government control.

He said privatisation, sluggish under the ex-communist administration, was picking up speed with 800 firms turned over to private hands in the past four months. That figure represented 25 percent of companies sold off from 1993 to 1996.
"We have no intention of hunting down guilty parties for the current situation," Ciorbea said. "We only want to find the light at the end of the tunnel."
Ciorbea also forecast lower inflation after large rises earlier this year prompted by jumps in the price of staple goods, petrol and utilities.
He revised downward to 4.5 percent a forecast for May inflation after predicting six percent last week.
Ciorbea's government has moved quickly to meet the demands of Western creditors, ramming through parliament an austerity budget and legislation to win over reluctant foreign investors.

The International Monetary Fund in April approved a $430 million loan package and the World Bank is expected on Tuesday to give formal backing to $625 million in credits for reforms, including benefits to help those hardest hit.
Average monthly salaries stand at less than $80, far below those in more developed Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- the countries Romanians like to emulate.

Ciorbea's ministers have acknowledged that the budget, calling for spending cuts and sharp reductions in subsidies, will have to be revised next month to account for price rises to date and planned tax cuts.
Plans to reduce the budget deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from last year's 5.8 percent are on target.

But analysts say the government's inflation targets, now set at 110 percent year-on-year for 1997, remain unrealistic in view of increases which pushed price increases to 89.5 percent in April from last December.
